We introduce a novel Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, designed to capture nonlinear dynamics and sudden shifts in data patterns. This model employs a time-varying coefficient for the autoregressive component, which is influenced by a moving average of past coefficients. We utilize a Bayesian approach to estimate the model parameters and apply Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for inference. Our analysis of simulated and real-world data sets reveals that the TV-PARX model effectively identifies the nonlinear and time-varying nature of the data, as well as any structural breaks present.

A novel method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) across a broad area using photometric data collected over a wide field of view is presented. This approach, which can be applied to various wide-field photometric systems without the need for absolute calibration, utilizes a multi-wavelength radiative transfer model to convert photometric measurements into AOds across a broad area. The method was tested using data from a five-wavelength system that monitors the sky within a 90-degree field of view, operating between 340 and 400 nm. The system, which has been in use since 2010, is part of the Norwegian Network for Continuous Optical Aerosol Monitoring (NORCAMS). The resulting AOds derived from the photometric data were found to be in close agreement with those obtained from a five-wavelength spectrometer installed on the system in 2016. The average difference between the AOds derived from the photometric and spectrometric data was 0.008, with a standard deviation of 0.020. The results demonstrate that wide-field photometric systems can be used to obtain broad-area AOds without the need for absolute calibration, making them valuable tools for studying aerosols on large scales.

This study investigates the simulation of a biomolecular system, specifically alanine dipeptide, using various numerical methods to solve the Liouville operator within a high-dimensional phase space. The research aims to determine the most computationally efficient method for an accurate simulation of the system's microcanonical dynamics. The numerical methods under examination include projection methods, such as the Fourier spectral method and Fast Fourier Transform, as well as finite difference methods, and splitting methods, including the Strang and higher-order splitting techniques. The research reveals that the finite difference method, specifically the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, offers the best balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. The findings also demonstrate that higher-order splitting methods, such as the fourth-order splitting technique, can achieve an accuracy comparable to the Fourier spectral method with a significantly reduced computational cost. The research contributes to the understanding of the simulation of biomolecular systems using phase space decomposition techniques and provides valuable insights for future research in the field.

This research project aims to develop more effective guidelines for creating training data for visually impaired users, focusing on training description systems. Despite the widespread use of image description systems, current standards for training data leave room for improvement, particularly in their relevance to end-users. As a contribution to this issue, we have created refined guidelines that are designed to be training data for an automatic abstract generator, specifically targeting the benefit of visually impaired users. These enhanced guidelines were incorporated into the existing training datasets, resulting in improved performance of training systems, demonstrating the training data's higher quality. The outcomes of this research project are intended to be utilized as a high-standard training dataset, contributing to the creation of more effective image description systems that benefit end-users.

This research paper explores the optimization problem in quantum field theory, specifically focusing on the mass renormalization scheme for the ghost field within the context of the Dyson-Schwinger equations. We utilize the Euler-Arnold framework to solve this problem, utilizing a ninth-order polynomial tensor basis. Initially, we employ a basic tensor grid, but we then apply the Euler-Arnold method to refine the minimization of the functional. We utilize various tensor basis truncation orders (second, third, and fourth) to solve the optimization problem at different values of momentum transfer. We present the resulting renormalization constants as functions of the dimensionless coupling constant for various truncation orders and momentum transfer values. We also conduct a comparison between the second and third-order truncation orders by fitting the renormalization constants to a coupling constant model, yielding a set of fitted parameters for the quantum field theory under consideration.

In the context of QCD, heavy quarks interact weakly and can form particles known as heavy quarkonium, which can be influenced by environmental conditions such as the temperature of a plasma. To investigate the behavior of these particles, a theoretical framework called the heavy quark potential is utilized, which can be calculated using perturbative methods at short distances and non-perturbative approaches like AdS/CFT at long distances. A specific model, the holographic heavy quark potential, is derived from the context of a strongly coupled N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills plasma and can be adapted to a more realistic quark-gluon plasma by adjusting the temperature and a running coupling constant. To account for the effects of screening in long-distance interactions, a screening mass is incorporated into the potential, and its optimal value can be determined by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data on particle production. Once the potential is established, the thermal decay of heavy quarkonium states can be calculated using the formalism of Matsui and Satz, and the resulting spectrum of surviving particles can be determined in heavy ion collisions. The results of these simulations can be compared to experimental data to validate the approach and explore the behavior of heavy quarkonium in the context of the quark-gluon plasma.

This research investigates the fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization problems in wideband waveforming, where multiple signals are transmitted across various frequency sub-bands to multiple users. The signal's quality is influenced by the combination of sub-bands a user is targeted with, and fairness is ensured by considering fair-throughput as the minimum value among all users. The problem of optimizing fair-throughput is found to be NP-hard, so a convex relaxation method is proposed to obtain a fair-throughput value close to the optimal. The research also examines the fair-throughput optimization problem under linear constraints, which is found to be tractable. The fair-throughput can be maximized by setting the sum-throughput to a value and optimizing it, and an efficient algorithm is developed to find the maximum fair-throughput value. The proposed fair-throughput optimization problem is shown to be equivalent to one with linear constraints, and the research provides insights into the relationship between fair-throughput and sum-throughput. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness.

This research paper presents a PDF fitting framework that utilizes the Tapestry and FastKNN libraries, and explores the TMD and LHC energy scales. The code is publicly available on GitHub. We conducted a PDF fit at the LHC scale, incorporating data from W, $t$bar$+$$t$, and $Z$ boson production, as well as DY and jet scattering processes, and the ABRAB10 NNLO scheme. The resulting PDFs were evaluated and plotted using the JetAsso code. Our results showed that our best-fit NNLO $Q^2$ scale of 2.00 GeV$^2$ aligns with NNLO predictions, and the NNLO and NLO$\\gamma G$ scheme produced similar outcomes. We also found that the N$^3$LO and NNLO ABRAB10 schemes produced similar results, and the TMD and LHC scales yielded comparable outcomes. Our findings contribute to the understanding of TMD and LHC scales, as well as NNLO and NLO$\\gamma G$ schemes.

A linearized framework is developed to analyze the behavior of reacting flows under turbulent conditions, focusing on a droplet evaporating and burning in an air stream. A state-space model is created by applying a small perturbation approach to the governing equations, utilizing a Burke-Schumann flame model and an enthalpy-based combustion model. To evaluate the model's effectiveness, a Monte Carlo simulation is performed on the linearized state-space model, comparing its output to the true system's response. Various factors are examined to determine their impact on the accuracy of the linearized model, including the linearization framework, the choice of unresolved model, and the characteristics of turbulent fluctuations. After a thorough analysis, the enthalpy-based combustion model is identified as the most suitable for the linearized state-space framework.

This study introduces a nonlocal gravity model that can be defined through an easily measurable quantity, departing from the conventional approach of using higher-order derivatives of the metric tensor. In this framework, the nonlocal gravity field is an easily observable quantity, similar to how electromagnetic fields are treated in physics. The proposed nonlocal gravity field is defined as an average of the Ricci tensor over a small region of spacetime, which can be expressed as an integral operator acting on the gravitational source. This nonlocal gravity field is then used to construct a nonlocal gravity potential that satisfies a nonlocal gravity Poisson equation. The resulting nonlocal gravity theory is shown to be equivalent to a higher-order derivative theory, which can be verified through the analysis of a free-falling particle's motion and the calculation of the de Sitter universe's dynamics. The nonlocal gravity field defined in this study is found to be an easily observable quantity, which can be directly measured in principle. This approach provides a new perspective on nonlocal gravity theories, which can be defined through easily measurable quantities, and may have implications for the study of dark energy and modified gravity theories.

With the possible formation of small quark-gluon droplets in high-energy, central proton-proton collisions, we may observe an increase in the production of strange quarks. This phenomenon, known as "surrender," has been observed in experiments at the LHC and is believed to be a precursor to the behavior seen in heavy ion collisions. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of strange and multi-strange baryon production in pp collisions at various energies, including single and double differential cross-sections for various baryon types. The data is compared to theoretical predictions from the Martin, DGLAP-MSSW, and KKP models, as well as the EPOS and HYDJET simulations. The results indicate that all parton distribution function (PDF) sets can accurately describe single differential data, while only the KKP and KKS sets can accurately model the energy dependence of the ratio of gluon to sea quark distributions. Additionally, the EPOS and HYDJET simulations are found to accurately reproduce the observed behavior of strange baryons, indicating a possible connection between baryon production and the transition from hadronic to partonic matter.

Determining the population of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) in the Milky Way is crucial for predicting the rate of gravitational wave events. While the number of active NS-LMXBs is well-known, the total count of systems, including inactive ones, remains uncertain. This study proposes a new method to estimate the number of hidden NS-LMXBs by examining the possible transformation of current radio pulsar LMXBs into inactive systems through accretion-induced spin-up to become millisecond radio pulsars. Using a standard model of the initial distribution of pulsar LMXBs, this approach predicts a total population of about 10^6 NS-LMXBs in the Milky Way, which is significantly higher than current estimates. This finding suggests that the conversion rate from pulsar LMXBs to millisecond radio pulsars is lower than typically assumed, or that the initial formation rate of pulsar LMXBs is higher than previously thought.

A bipartite graph can be drawn in a planar manner by dividing a vertex into multiple points, with the number of divisions bounded by a function of the graph's aspect ratio. This limit is derived from the aspect ratio, and the graph's embedding within the point set is polynomially computable. The method involves a recursive process that divides a square area containing the drawing into smaller squares, with each smaller square containing a portion of the divided vertex. This approach builds upon a previous algorithm that can also embed a graph with no cycles into a square grid, but with a linear increase in the aspect ratio.

A compromised system's performance can be manipulated to make it more vulnerable to data access attacks, such as Flush+Reload. While this technique is effective, its success relies on significant slowdowns and a large number of compromised traces. In contrast, a new attack strategy called HyperDegrade builds upon Flush+Reload by using Hyperthreading to isolate traceable memory areas more effectively, leading to enhanced data recovery. When evaluated against Flush+Reload, HyperDegrade results in a 100-fold increase in the amount of accessible data, requires a tenfold reduction in the number of compromised traces, and can be accomplished with a more precise analysis of traceable areas. In practical tests, HyperDegrade achieved the same level of data access as Flush+Reload with a tenfold reduction in time spent on the attack, or the same time spent with a tenfold increase in data access capabilities.

A new type of knotted structure called a diagonal knot has been defined within the context of link diagrams. This structure can be obtained from a standard knot by incorporating a diagonal move, which is a specific transformation that can be applied to the knot diagram. It has been demonstrated that this diagonal move is equivalent to a sequence of standard Reidemeister moves, combined with a bypass move and a twist/untwist move, all of which can be achieved through isotopy. Building on this finding, a version of the Jones polynomial has been developed specifically for diagonal knots. Moreover, it has been shown that the diagonal move can be detected through the polynomial, which can be achieved by applying specific operators to the diagram. As a result, the polynomial can be used to distinguish between various structures that are not equivalent, including a notable example where a modified $5_2$ knot with one crossing added and a figure-eight knot with one crossing added are not equivalent when considering diagonal knots.

In a multi-agent learning environment, agents with varying levels of sophistication compete to predict the outcomes of complex tasks, where simple prediction is free but accurate prediction incurs a cost. This paper investigates how the distribution of task difficulties influences the behavior of agents, particularly in a two-agent system with linear costs. We find that agents with different sophistication levels adopt threshold-based strategies, and the difficulty distribution significantly impacts prediction accuracy, learning costs, and the choice of optimal strategies. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a multiple-agent system with linear costs, demonstrating that optimal strategies remain threshold-based under certain conditions.

A Cartesian decomposition of a set $X$ is defined as a collection of equivalence relations on $X$ that act regularly and commute with one another. This paper focuses on the case where the equivalence relations are derived from groups, and we explore the connection between regular group actions and the structure of the set. We provide a unified framework for various known results, including those concerning affine spaces, spaces acted upon by product groups, and spaces acted upon by twisted product groups. Furthermore, we introduce a new characterization of sets acted upon by powers of diagonal groups. A concise summary of this new result is as follows: Let $G$ be a finite group of size $n$, and let $D_n$ denote the diagonal group formed by the action of $G$ on its $k$-th power. Then, the set of all commuting $k$-tuples of $G$ is equivalent to a space acted upon by the $k$-th power of the diagonal group in a Cartesian decomposition with $k!n^{k-1}$ components, each corresponding to a distinct action of $G$ on its $k$-th power.

A novel design for an interferometer, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, has been proposed to overcome limitations in traditional Sagnac and Mach-Zehnder interferometer configurations regarding sensitivity to certain types of noise. By varying the power flow within the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a significant improvement in sensitivity to length changes can be achieved without compromising the operating point's stability against optical power fluctuations. A theoretical analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's behavior under different operating conditions reveals that this design can be optimized to be highly sensitive to external disturbances, similar to the techniques used in advanced LIGO and GEO600 gravitational wave detectors. A simulation of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's performance indicates that this design can be used to create an effective 10 km long gravitational wave detector using only a 1-meter long interferometer, demonstrating its potential for creating large-scale detectors in compact spaces.

In response to the growing demand for high data rates, massive XL-MIMO systems have been developed, but they face challenges with random access delays. To address this issue, we introduce a novel random access protocol called NOVR-XL, designed specifically for XL-MIMO systems. Our protocol leverages the potential of extended time and space dimensions, utilizing a hybrid approach that combines time-based and power-based reductions. Our proposed protocol optimizes random access performance by reducing unnecessary transmissions, resulting in improved success rates and lower access delays. Through theoretical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our protocol, which outperforms existing methods, especially in scenarios with high traffic loads.

This research paper explores the integration of n-gram models and neural language models for machine translation evaluation and summarization quality assessment. Although neural language models have shown significant improvements in tasks like machine translation evaluation and summarization quality assessment, n-gram models continue to play a crucial role. We propose a framework that combines n-gram and neural language models using a linear combination approach. Our experiments on low-resource languages demonstrate that this combination can lead to better performance in both machine translation evaluation and summarization quality assessment.

In 2020, the vote tabulation system used in Belgium faced an issue where an incorrect entry of '3' instead of '8' on ballot scanners led to a false report of third-party candidates winning the election. To enhance the reliability of similar systems, particularly in contexts like Belgian elections where candidates write their names rather than select from a list, an improved system based on existing one is proposed. This improved system incorporates an optimized spell-checking algorithm that functions as an automatic error-correction mechanism for mistakes made during the scanning process, treating such mistakes as unrecognized characters. The effectiveness of this new system is demonstrated through results from a test set consisting of ballot templates and erroneous entries resulting from simulated errors, showing nearly 100% accuracy in restoring the original text. The underlying assumption is that vote counts remain unchanged despite character errors, enabling verification of correct text reconstruction through vote count consistency. The success of this system in accurately recovering compromised Belgian election ballots highlights its potential application in various optical character recognition tasks dealing with data where numerical values are critical.

A simplified atmospheric model for an Earth-like atmosphere is used to investigate the circulation patterns that emerge under the conditions found on Mars. When the Earth-like atmosphere is subjected to the strong temperature differences observed on Mars during the winter season, baroclinic storms develop in the polar regions, mimicking the behavior seen on Mars. These storms consist of warm air advection at higher altitudes and cold air advection at lower levels, creating warm and cold pools in the polar regions similar to those observed on Mars. The circulation patterns observed in the model are consistent with the patterns seen in the Mars atmosphere, particularly the reversal of winds at the 300 mbar level and the formation of storm systems in the polar regions during the winter season. The findings suggest that the circulation patterns seen on Mars are driven by seasonal changes in solar heating, rather than the composition of the atmosphere. The results also provide a foundation for studying the atmosphere's response to changes in carbon dioxide levels and the development of seasonal features on Mars.

This research explores the complex representation of the Gamma function through contour integration, specifically along a Hankel path. By employing a novel approach to manipulate the integrand, we derive fresh integral representations of the Gamma function that are applicable for all positive real numbers. These new integrals are shown to satisfy the Gamma function's recurrence relation, leading to a straightforward proof of the same property. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our newly defined Gamma function and the classical one proposed by Barnes.

A linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme is proposed to enhance linearized quantum hydrodynamic methods for simulating strongly correlated quantum systems. This new approach incorporates a stochastic noise source that evolves according to a hydrodynamic equation, thereby accounting for a more accurate description of quantum fluctuations. This method is particularly suitable for systems with slow-varying quantum correlations, such as nearly superfluid quantum gases. A key advantage of this scheme is its ability to simulate nonequilibrium quantum correlations without incurring high-frequency oscillations that typically plague traditional split-operator methods. As a proof of concept, this linearized linearized quantum hydrodynamic scheme is applied to a sudden expansion of a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate, demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating nonequilibrium quantum correlations. Furthermore, this scheme can be extended to describe nonequilibrium spin dynamics by incorporating a spin hydrodynamic equation, thereby enabling the simulation of nonequilibrium spin correlations.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have grown so large that their deployment on devices with limited resources is challenging. To address this issue, knowledge distillation has emerged as a technique where a compact student network learns from a larger teacher network. While many Teacher-Student architectures have been developed, they often require significant modifications to the teacher network to suit the student network, which can compromise the teacher's performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose a framework called Self-Organizing Teacher (SOT), which allows a pre-trained deep teacher network to adapt its structure to better fit a lightweight student network without any changes to the Teacher-Student architecture. By utilizing an attention mechanism, the student network can dynamically adjust the teacher network's structure in real-time, resulting in an efficient and adaptable "big model" for the student network. We tested our framework on various Teacher-Student combinations using ImageNet, demonstrating that the SOT can match or outperform statically adjusted teacher networks with little extra computation.

Graphical models, particularly those representing probability distributions, are crucial for understanding complex real-world scenarios. An effective algorithm, Bucket Elimination, is fundamental to inferring and optimizing these models, both in their raw and logarithmic forms. This algorithm's power lies in its ability to project onto marginal distributions, enabling enhanced versions that integrate cutting planes and convex relaxations for more accurate results. These improvements can be optimized using techniques like bound tightening, leading to a suite of methods that provide increasingly precise outcomes. Our research introduces a novel, iterative Bucket Elimination approach that combines optimization steps, resulting in an algorithm with polynomial time complexity that guarantees convergence to the most accurate possible outcomes. This method, which can be implemented in various forms such as logarithmic and raw data, as well as through different convex relaxations like Chow-Liu and positive graphical models, stands out for its practicality and efficiency.

An explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is provided for all $n \geq 0$. By applying Newton's identities, we can derive an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{gl}_d)$ for all $d \geq 0$ and $n \geq 0$. Furthermore, we can obtain an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{so}_d)$ for all $d \geq 0$ and $n \geq 0$ by utilizing the relation between the centralizers of special orthogonal groups and general linear groups.

An exact algorithm for implementing the paired-permutation test has been developed using Monte Carlo methods. An initial exact algorithm proposed by Stanley in 1986 is enhanced to increase its efficiency significantly. By integrating a technique from Nijenhuis and Reeds from 1970, an improved algorithm is created that reduces time complexity from factorial to a lower factorial rate. The improved exact algorithm produces paired-permutation distributions for large datasets, demonstrating close agreement with Monte Carlo-based distributions.

A notable trend has been observed in recent research on the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow $v_3$ and elliptic flow $v_2$ in heavy ion collisions. This trend, which was seen in data from Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various energies, is also present in $p$+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 8.16$ TeV, as measured by the STAR collaboration. The pattern is evident across different particle species, including pions, kaons, and protons. A theoretical model, the AMY-ArcHMHy, is found to accurately predict this trend, which is attributed to the similar underlying mechanisms of $v_2$ and $v_n$ generation, as well as their dependence on the medium's response to initial anisotropy. The model's success in replicating the trend suggests that future research on the transverse momentum dependence of $v_2$ and $v_n$ in high multiplicity $p$+Pb collisions could provide valuable insights into the quark-gluon plasma's properties.

Recently, there has been growing interest in using multiple sensors to detect and track targets that are not always visible within their limited fields of view. A key challenge in this task is the high computational cost of searching through all possible movements of the sensors. A new approach called the Nested Monte Carlo (NMC) estimator was proposed to address this challenge, which uses a sequential importance sampling method to estimate the probability of a target's presence in a given area. A nested Monte carlo process is then used to estimate the probability of a sensor's field of view covering a given area. A unique feature of this proposed method is that it can be optimized without the need to discretize the target's movement patterns, which can be computationally expensive. A comparison of the proposed Nested Monte Carlo (NMC) and Nested Sequential Importance Sampling (NSIS) estimators shows that they have the same level of bias and variance, but the NMC estimator can be more efficient to compute. A simulation study was also conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed Nested Monte Carlo (NMC) estimator in a scenario where sensors are searching for targets that are not always visible within their limited fields of view. The results show that the proposed Nested Monte Carlo (NMC) estimator can effectively track targets that are not always detectable, even when using a single sensor, and can also be extended to multiple sensors without significantly increasing computational complexity.

In soccer games, the decision-making process for a player who has gained possession of the ball is complicated by the fact that various actions like passing, shooting, dribbling, fouling, and letting the ball go out of bounds all have different rewards and risks, which can change during the game. To address this challenge, we developed a deep recurrent neural network model that predicts the reward of each action in any given game situation, taking into account the fact that action rewards can vary dynamically. We also designed a policy learning algorithm that uses these predicted rewards to determine the best course of action for the player. To train our model, we used data from soccer games that had been annotated with actions and their outcomes, and we tested it on two real games to see how well it worked. Our tests showed that our action-value function can distinguish between situations where fouling or letting the ball go out of bounds might be better than shooting, and where passing or dribbling might be better than shooting, demonstrating the importance of considering all possible actions when making decisions in soccer games.

Recent events have led to heightened experimental setup automation needs, triggered by reduced travel and increased telework requirements. This situation presents an opportunity to explore the potential of remote laboratory experiments. This paper provides an overview of remote lab experiments, focusing on their relevance to particle physics and astrophysics, and outlines key challenges and possible solutions. The authors propose a set of guidelines for designing and implementing remote lab experiments, which can be applied to various physics disciplines. The paper also highlights the benefits of these experiments, such as improved data sharing, collaboration, and education, and notes their connection to open science principles. The authors believe that remote lab experiments can serve as a foundation for fully open experiments, which would be accessible to everyone, including students, and could be a model for future physics experiments.

A one-dimensional system is considered consisting of a harmonic and an anharmonic oscillator, with the anharmonic oscillator initially displaced from its equilibrium position. The system's solitary waves are analyzed for their stability in a rotating reference frame. The governing equations are derived from the Euler-Poisson model, with pressure described by an ideal gas law. It is found that solitary waves can be generated in the system and that their oscillation patterns are stable and predictable. The waves' oscillation frequencies are determined to be influenced by the anharmonic oscillator's presence, with the frequencies being non-linear and not following a simple harmonic pattern. The results are supported by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, demonstrating the system's ability to produce solitary waves with stable and predictable oscillation patterns.

A neutral long-lived particle (NLSP) produced in high-energy collisions at a collider can decay further into detectable particles within a certain distance from the interaction point. The decay length of this particle can vary greatly, from fractions of a millimeter to several kilometers, and this range significantly affects the design of searches for such particles at colliders. A typical example of such a particle is a neutralino that can decay into a gravitino at the Large Hadron Collider. In this scenario, the most effective detection methods involve using all data from the experiment, including events that appear to be missing energy, regardless of whether the neutralino decays or not. However, if the neutralino decays into a gravitino over a longer distance, the detection strategy needs to focus on events that are missing less energy and have fewer events that are consistent with the events that are not detected. In this case, the ability to identify such events depends on the distance over which the neutralino decays, and a variety of methods can be used to determine this distance, including detectors that are placed further away from the interaction point, muon chambers that are located even further, and muons that are identified by their curvature in a magnetic field.

This study investigates the role of context in language evolution by analyzing the interpretations of words that underwent semantic shifts on the SWEARD dataset as their contextual variability changes. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, we discovered that altering contextual variance has little impact on model predictions for most semantic shifts, with the exception of contextual bias-driven changes. To address this, we developed a modified approach that takes into account the variance of the surrounding context before mapping it to the model's input space. Our findings indicate that this new method yields more accurate results for contextual bias-driven changes, highlighting the importance of context in these types of evolutions.

A significant portion of dark matter is hypothesized to be composed of ultra-light particles, which may manifest as oscillating classical fields on macroscopic scales. This research presents stringent constraints on the mass spectrum of dark matter consisting of ultra-light particles, with the exception of a small range between 10^-17 and 10^-16 eV. This research leverages data from the LIGO and Virgo detectors, specifically from the S1900006-GW event, which involved a neutron star merger. This analysis examines a variety of dark matter models, including axions, oscillating axion monodromy, and various types of ultra-light scalar and bosonic dark matter. The findings are particularly relevant to the no-hair theorem, which predicts that neutron stars merging would emit dark matter until they lose their distinctive properties. This research also considers the impact of the resulting cloud of dark matter on the structure of dark matter halos and the detection of it as dark radiation. This research extends previous research by considering a more comprehensive survey of ultra-light particle models and by utilizing the data from the LIGO and Virgo detectors, which has a heightened sensitivity to the oscillating fields.

Quantum driven systems typically deviate from their initial coherent state due to nonlinear dynamics, leading to the emergence of non-classical properties such as state fragmentation and synchronization. This research investigates the application of the optimized mean-field method to the forced Sargent model, demonstrating its capacity to accurately predict synchronization and fragmentation patterns observed in this system. Furthermore, this approach can be extended to various nonlinear quantum systems, including the Sargent model, by utilizing multi-component coherent states.

Quantum relational Hoare logic serves as a framework for specifying and verifying the behavior of quantum programs, particularly focusing on how inputs relate to outputs. This paper provides a concise overview of quantum relational Hoare logic, delving into the challenges of using it for input-output specification and verification. A key contribution is the development of a quantitative variant, which allows for precise determination of how a program's input-output relationship aligns with specified relations. This approach relies on the representation of relations as operators acting on the input Hilbert space, utilizing the concept of fidelity to measure the closeness of the actual and desired input-output relationships. A specific case study is presented to illustrate the application of this variant, demonstrating its effectiveness in practical scenarios.

To accurately analyze vector magnetic field maps, it's crucial to account for magnetic fill fraction, especially when studying small-scale magnetic fields on the Sun's surface. An automated system has been developed to explicitly account for magnetic fill fraction in vector magnetic field maps, which are typically measured with the Inverse Spectroscopy Method (ISM). By utilizing a grid search algorithm to optimize vector magnetic field maps, the system can generate an output that is an explicit vector magnetic field map that takes into account magnetic fill fraction. The system's performance was evaluated using synthetic vector magnetic field maps with known values of magnetic field strength and direction, as well as real vector magnetic field maps from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The results showed that explicitly accounting for magnetic fill fraction can significantly improve vector magnetic field map accuracy, especially when dealing with small-scale magnetic fields. The system's code is publicly available on GitHub, and the authors believe that vector magnetic field maps that explicitly account for magnetic fill fraction can provide a more accurate representation of the Solar Observatory's global magnetic field and are suitable for large-scale vector magnetic field forecasting models.

In the context of a Coxeter group, we explore the connection between the number of spheres within a specific region of the group's Artin monoid and the dimensions of its generating set. When the region is defined by spheres corresponding to subsets of the generating set, we find that the number of spheres in this region is equivalent to the count of subsets that do not contain any subsets from the defining subset. We apply this combinatorial approach to examine the region defined by subsets of {s,t,u}, demonstrating that the region's structure varies based on the Coxeter group's type.

A curve whose osculating plane consistently coincides with its binormal plane is known as a Bertrand curve. 
Initially defined in Euclidean space by Bertrand in 1850, this concept has since been extended to various non-Euclidean spaces, including semi-Euclidean spaces and spaces with varying metrics. 
This paper provides a unified definition of Bertrand curves for spaces with arbitrary metrics, revealing that they are well-defined in both spaces with a signature of (p,0) and those with a signature of (0,p). 
Building on this definition, the paper investigates the properties of Bertrand curves in space with a signature of (p,1), deriving their characterization and providing examples. 
Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between Bertrand and tubular curves in the same space, concluding that they are equivalent. 
Finally, the paper derives the parametric equations for the transform of a Bertrand curve under a conformal change of metric.

Multi-task learning has gained popularity in natural language processing due to the ease of combining various tasks that utilize the same input and output formats. However, in scenarios where inputs and outputs have different representations, such as translation tasks, under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence may hinder the effectiveness of multi-task learning. To address this issue, we propose a technique called Multi-Task Learning with Reweighted Gradient Descent (MTRGD) that adjusts the learning rates of various tasks to balance their optimization. We tested MTRGD on three different datasets using three commonly used loss functions to evaluate its effectiveness. Our findings demonstrate that simple learning rate adjustments can achieve comparable or even better results than complex multi-task optimization methods. Additionally, we found that in Coherent Phrase Translation, under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence may hinder multi-task learning performance compared to more commonly used options like MSE. To mitigate this issue, we recommend using MSE as the optimization objective for MT and SST tasks while using KL Divergence for CPT, which yields the best results.

Program induction involves creating new rules from existing examples, which can be represented as (input, output) pairs. A notable application of this concept is the "if-then" programming task, where both inputs and outputs are structured as hierarchical natural language sentences. A neural model that aims to input one part of the example and output the other part is challenged by the vast number of possible sentence structures. To address this, a neural model that inputs the missing portion of the example's output can be trained on the hierarchical structure of possible "if-then" relation types. The research findings reveal that training on this structure can significantly enhance the model's performance, and combining this structure with the inputs' semantic information through attention mechanisms can further boost results. The research outcomes demonstrate that training on the hierarchical structure of relation types can help the model generalize to unseen relation types, and a system built on this approach has achieved state-of-the-art results on a few-shot induction task on the RuleTaker dataset.

This research proposes a novel method for predicting videos from novel viewpoints using multi-view inputs from known viewpoints, leveraging a dual representation that combines linear and non-linear components. The linear component utilizes a basis that aligns with the underlying structure of videos, while the non-linear component employs a predictor that accounts for the intricate relationship between videos and camera viewpoints. By iteratively updating the dual variables, our approach achieves convergence to an optimal solution, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods on several benchmark datasets.

A graph's metric dimension can be modified by limiting the geodesic distance within the graph to a specific value. Initially, we define a truncated version of the graph's distance metric, and then we define a new concept called the metric dimension of the truncated graph. We find that for certain types of graphs, particularly regular graphs, the truncated metric dimension is usually the same as the original metric dimension, with a few possible higher values. We also develop an algorithm to calculate the possible higher values for any given graph and apply it to determine the truncated metric dimension for various graphs.

This study introduces a novel approach for identifying heart sound abnormalities in noisy environments using a transformer-based model, without the need for pre-processing noisy data or using noisy samples during training.

To investigate the role of low-density molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoirs in extreme starburst galaxies, we analyzed the ratios of CI line emissions at 3.69 and 0.89 micrometers, denoted as RCI, for a sample of 18 galaxies. These ratios were compared with a suite of hydrodynamic simulations, specifically the MAGMA project, which modeled a variety of starburst scenarios. Our findings reveal that the inclusion of a circumgalactic gas reservoir significantly reduces the predicted infrared emission from highly excited CI+, resulting in an $R_{CI}$ value that is comparable to observed values. On the other hand, a molecular wind alone is insufficient to account for the lower infrared emission from CI+, unless the wind velocity is extremely high, which is unlikely. However, a combination of a circumgas reservoir and a weak molecular wind can produce an $R_{CI}$ value that mimics the impact of a molecular wind alone. We propose that the CI lines serve as an indicator of the presence of a circumgalactic gas reservoir in starburst galaxies, and an $D_{10}$ to $R_{CI}$ ratio greater than 3 suggests the presence of such a reservoir.

This study investigates the velocity distribution of a second class particle in an asymmetric exclusion process on a one-dimensional lattice, where incoming particles at the boundaries have equal density. We derive the distribution's recurrence relation and express it as a combination of Poisson distributions. By employing a generating function approach, we obtain a closed-form expression for the velocity distribution at discrete time points. As time progresses, the Poisson distribution components decouple, leading to a power law decay of the velocity distribution at infinity. Our findings align with previously obtained results for a single block initial condition and enable the determination of the particle's current distribution.

In epidemiology, fitting mathematical models to data is a common practice, particularly with the surge in sharing epidemiological data and models during a pandemic. While many models are based on differential equations, it's crucial to ensure the parameters fitted are biologically feasible. This paper introduces a new approach to incorporating such constraints into the fitting process, using an example of an SIR model fitted to COVID-19 data. The method involves representing the feasible parameter space as a convex polyhedron and utilizing projection techniques within the optimization process. The proposed technique is evaluated through both synthetic data experiments and real-world data experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness. The code is made available on GitHub for further use.

A significant break in the relationship between galaxy mass and NUV-r color is observed, particularly for galaxies with stellar masses exceeding 10^10.2 solar masses. This phenomenon is attributed to the emergence of star-forming blue cloud galaxies at the high-mass end of the mass spectrum. Our findings are based on a sample of 1000 galaxies with stellar masses ranging from 10^7 to 10^11 solar masses, all within a redshift range of 0 to 0.15, as observed through deep imaging conducted by the VIMOS spectrograph. The color-mass relation derived from this sample aligns well with previous studies, albeit with a more pronounced break at the blue end of the spectrum for more massive galaxies. The break's presence is further corroborated by fitting a two-component Schechter function to the NUV-r color distribution, which yields a power-law slope of 1.5 for galaxies with NUV-r colors greater than 1.0. The break's occurrence at a mass of approximately 10^10.2 solar masses coincides with the inflection point in the stellar mass function, suggesting that the formation of star-forming blue cloud galaxies at the massive end of the spectrum is responsible for the NUV-r color-mass relation's behavior at the high-mass end.

This research investigates the effectiveness of using multilingual sentiment data to enhance the capabilities of a Chinese sentiment analysis model through few-shot learning. The study utilizes the Massive Multilingual Knowledge Corpus (MMLU) and finds that pre-training a state-of-the-art Chinese sentiment model with multilingual sentiment data yields promising results. The research also explores the use of language embeddings to map multilingual sentiment labels to the target language and discovers that using only English sentiment labels yields comparable performance to using the corresponding Chinese labels. The study concludes that leveraging multilingual sentiment data can be an effective strategy for improving the capabilities of a target language model.

A star exhibiting atypical behavior was identified as a possible new class of variable stars through a survey of the Kepler data. The star in question, designated KIC 9267654, is a rapidly rotating F-type main sequence star that displays a puzzling rotation profile. Initially, the star exhibited a sinusoidal variability pattern with a period of 0.3 days and a depth of 0.1 magnitudes. However, the period subsequently increased to 0.4 days and then to 0.5 days over a span of 100 days. To investigate the unusual profile, a comprehensive analysis of possible causes was conducted, including tidal interactions, pulsations, and magnetic activity. The most plausible explanation for the observed behavior is a gradual slowdown in the star's rotation rate, possibly due to the development of a magnetic activity cycle similar to the Sun's. To verify this hypothesis, a theoretical model was developed to predict the evolution of a star's rotation period as it undergoes an activity cycle. The model's output was found to be consistent with the observed profile of KIC 9267654, suggesting the possibility of activity cycles occurring on other stars as well. The discovery of such cycles on other stars could provide valuable insights into the physics governing stellar magnetic activity and its connection to rotation and convection.

Fake news poses a significant threat to social stability and democratic processes, prompting the need for effective real-time detection systems. While deep learning-based methods have shown promise in reducing misinformation, their reliance on labeled data limits their effectiveness, especially in cases where information is scarce. To address this challenge, the MetaFEND model combines few-shot learning with meta-learning to enable few-shot cross-domain few-shot learning. By utilizing few-shot learning to adapt to new domains and meta-learning to quickly adapt to new tasks, the MetaFEND model can effectively detect fake news in new domains and for new tasks with limited data. Experimental results on three large-scale datasets demonstrate the MetaFEND model's superior performance compared to various state-of-the-art approaches.

A quaternary Golay complementary array pair is a unique arrangement of integers in a two-dimensional grid that has significant applications in signal processing and array theory. Determining the feasible sizes for these arrays is a challenging problem, but a recent study provides a comprehensive solution. This research demonstrates that a quaternary Golay complementary array pair of a specific size is possible if and only if the size meets a particular condition, which is either even or divisible by four. Additionally, specific feasible sizes are explicitly identified, including a range of sizes that are multiples of eight and several sizes that are not. These findings are significant as they contribute to the understanding of array theory and signal processing, and the proof relies on constructing feasible arrays through a combination of existing feasible arrays and symmetries.

This research presents a region segmentation approach tailored for medical imaging, specifically targeting MRI scans, using a two-step process. Initially, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) identifies the general area of interest, and then a Deep Neural Network (DNN) refines the region's boundaries. The study focuses on detecting and segmenting lesions in Multiple Sclerosis patients, but the method is applicable to various medical imaging tasks. The proposed technique outperforms existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This research introduces a novel framework called Unified Feature Extraction (UFE), which integrates unsupervised and supervised learning methods into a single model. Initially, we develop an unsupervised version of UFE that learns basic representations through contrastive learning. Building on this foundation, we then propose a supervised variant that incorporates label information to refine feature representation. We further derive a closed-form solution for the optimized parameters of linear supervised features. To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we conduct experiments on multiple image datasets using various downstream tasks. The results demonstrate that our unified feature extraction method outperforms existing approaches.

A recent trend in representation learning involves pre-training models on structured knowledge, specifically using factual triples from knowledge graphs, with the goal of enhancing natural language understanding. This approach has led to the development of KG-BERT, a model that is trained on structured knowledge and then applied to various tasks. However, it remains unclear how well models that are pre-trained on traditional text-based data, such as BERT, perform in comparison to those pre-trained on structured knowledge, particularly in terms of fact-based question-answering tasks. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by introducing a model that is pre-trained on structured knowledge, called KRoBERTa, and then fine-tuning it on various tasks. The KRoBERTa model is trained on structured knowledge, specifically using a knowledge graph, and then fine-tuned on various tasks. The results obtained from this fine-tuning process demonstrate that the KRoBERTa model performs on par with, and in some cases better than, traditional BERT-based models, particularly when it comes to knowledge graph-based tasks.

This study investigates the thermal profile and shadow dimensions of black holes within the framework of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter. The research focuses on three black hole types: the AdS-Schwarzschild black hole, the dyonic black hole, and the AdS-RN black hole. The analysis reveals that the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter has a non-linear impact on the thermal profile and shadow dimensions of black holes, resulting in an expansion of the thermal profile and an increase in shadow dimensions. The non-linear effect is more pronounced with higher charge values. The research also finds that the non-linear effect diminishes as the charge of the black hole increases, and the effect is more pronounced in the AdS-Schwarzschild black hole compared to the dyonic black hole. The research highlights the potential of thermal profile and shadow dimensions as observables for exploring the impact of non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter. The findings contribute to the understanding of the relationship between geometry and charge in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

Quantum phenomena such as entanglement and its increase have optical tomograms of entangled optical fields as their measurable indicators. This paper explores the connection between these nonclassical effects and the optical tomograms, focusing on the information-theoretic approach to quantifying them. We demonstrate that entanglement and its increase are linked to the optical tomograms' non-Gaussian and nonclassical characteristics. By analyzing Gaussian and non-Gaussian, single-field and multi-field quantum states, we show that information-theoretic criteria for assessing these nonclassical features align with the Susskind-Witten and Belavin-Polyakov-Milev-Savvidy theorems. This indicates that non-Gaussian and nonclassical properties of optical tomograms are essential for entanglement and its increase.

In a study conducted at the Belle experiment, the branching fractions for the decays of B^0_d mesons into D_s^- and a phi meson, as well as D_s^- and the conjugate phi meson, were measured for the first time. The branching fraction formula for B^0_d to D_s^- phi and B^0_d to D_s^- bar{phi} are both 0.6% uncertain due to particle physics factors, with a 1.3% uncertainty from experimental conditions. These results provide crucial data for understanding the weak decay mechanisms of bottom quarks and the intrinsic properties of charm-strange mesons.

To reconstruct the lattice of submodules of a module's module category, we assume the category is of finite dimension over an algebra that is multiplicity-free. In this context, we focus on a specific submodule lattice structure that has a composition factor of a certain type appearing once. We examine how this structure relates to the rest of the composition factors and determine the lattice's structure based on these relationships. In doing so, we discover that this specific submodule lattice structure is either isomorphic to a known lattice or contributes a projective line to the intersection of certain submodules within the lattice.

Recurrent curvature conditions have been extensively examined in Euclidean space, with a focus on biharmonic hypersurfaces. A recurrent operator is defined as one where the second derivative is equivalent to the initial operator, scaled by a positive function. A key question arises: does this condition of recurrence suffice to establish the same biharmonic hypersurface condition as the mean curvature? A counterexample is provided to demonstrate that the recurrence of the operator is insufficient. A new condition is then introduced, which guarantees the same biharmonic hypersurface condition.

We provide a Poincare series formula for subsets of d-space that are p/q recognizable, extending Nivat's theorem to non-integer dilations. This new p/q-Nivat theorem is derived from a p/q-Schnirelmann theorem, which is obtained through a connection between subsets' recognition properties and their image p/q-reducibility. We also establish that subsets p/q recognizable in one dimension are semilinear, and then use induction to prove the p/q-Nivat theorem.

This paper presents a unified formalism that extends the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) approach to derive bounds on semileptonic meson decay rates, building upon the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) framework. Within this new BGL-FBN system, form factors are expressed as power series in the momentum transfer variable, with coefficients constrained by positivity conditions and two-point correlation function bounds. These constraints allow for the determination of maximum possible decay rate ranges, which can be further refined using additional data. Applying these limits to semileptonic B to pi, K, D, and S decay channels reveals that the ranges predicted by the BGL-FBN system align with those from the CLN framework, with the exception of the K to l nu decay channel, where the BGL-FBN approach predicts a broader range. To narrow down these bounds, we examined the impact of varying the bounds on positive definite operators and found that tighter constraints on these bounds result in more precise decay rate predictions.

A dynamical system is deemed chaotic when a specific observable exhibits sensitivity to initial conditions over time, as measured by a positive Lyapunov exponent. In the context of general relativity, the AdS/CFT correspondence suggests that the conjectured universal bound on the growth rate of nearby geodesics applies to both the boundary field theory and the anti-de Sitter space. This paper aims to verify this equivalence by demonstrating that the universal bound on the Lyapunov exponent holds for a class of second-order conformal field theory operators, specifically those that are not conserved, within the large central charge limit. This proof relies on the holographic dual description of these operators as short-lived, nearly straight-line trajectories in the bulk, and utilizes the universal bound on the mixing of quantum states in the CFT.

In a recent study, a generalization of the angle function to higher-dimensional spaces of constant curvature was proposed, specifically hyperbolic and spherical spaces. This generalization is shown to retain key properties, leading to new results about the shape of domains in these spaces that can be conformally mapped into Euclidean space. Notably, complex domains in hyperbolic space that are conformally embeddable into Euclidean space were characterized based on boundary conditions, and domains in spherical space that are embeddable were also defined based on geometric properties. These results highlight the significance of generalized conformal geometry in understanding the shape of domains in constant curvature spaces.

To address the limitations of existing certification methods for point cloud models in face of twisting transformations, we have developed the Point Cloud Transformation Certification (TPC) framework. This framework enables the construction of certified defenses against twisting transformations and the development of certification algorithms that can accurately assess the robustness of robustified point cloud models. We have evaluated various robustification techniques, including local cleaning, global downsampling, and twisting-aware training, to determine their effectiveness in improving model robustness. Our experiments demonstrate that our framework can effectively apply existing methods to create twisting-robust models and develop certification algorithms that can accurately assess their performance. In comparison to baseline point cloud transformation certification algorithms, our framework results in significantly improved and certified accuracy against twisting transformations. Additionally, we have developed new, fully-adaptive and linear-time certified training approaches that can further enhance the robustness of models against twisting transformations. Our framework has been integrated into the PyTorch Geometric Library, making it easily accessible to researchers and practitioners.

In a collaborative debugging setting, a computerized system called TestUML aids programmers in identifying and fixing code issues. This test management tool provides an integrated testing environment that automatically presents debugging information to aid in the debugging process. When a code error is detected, the algorithm responsible for test generation can pinpoint the source of the error, propose a fix, and then continue testing to verify the correction. This feature is particularly valuable as it saves time and effort by eliminating the need to manually search through stack traces to identify the cause of a failure.

In our previous work, we introduced the concept of a $G_K$-Artin-Scheier cocycle and demonstrated its ability to recover the reduction modulo $p$ of a crystalline extension. Building on this, we now define a more general version of the $G_K$-Artin-Scheier cocycle, called the $G_K$-Artin-Scheier cocycle, which is defined on a broader class of extensions. We then introduce a specific type of this generalized cocycle, the $G_K$-A-CS cocycle, which is equivalent to the $G_K$-Artin-Scheier cocycle when the extension is crystalline.

This research investigates the use of a neuroevolutionary approach to optimize voltage patterns for damage detection in self-sensing composite materials. Using a piezoelectric sensor embedded within the material, the system converts strain data into electrical signals that are analyzed to identify and locate damage. A neuroevolutionary algorithm optimizes voltage patterns applied to the piezoelectric sensor to enhance the resulting current patterns' ability to detect damage. Experiments conducted on a plain weave carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) plate with and from damage caused by impact demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. Results show that while impact-induced damage results in changes in the self-sensing material's response, plain impacts produce subtle changes that are difficult to detect. However, when voltage patterns are optimized, even minor damage is easily identified and its location accurately pinpointed. The neuroevolutionary approach proves to be an effective alternative to traditional damage detection methods, providing a cost-effective and efficient solution for composite materials.

This research introduces vector-based integral identities that are geometric in nature and proves two new identities that are essential for calculating angular momentum operators in angular momentum eigenstates.

We define a specific type of action on trees for a group known as the right-angled Artin group associated with a graph that is not connected. This action is characterized by a tree with a finite set of branches, where the group's rank on each branch corresponds to the subgraph's induced structure. We find that a right subgraph that is not connected leads to this action's action on the tree's ends being divided into distinct segments, with the number of segments matching the components of the subgraph. Furthermore, we discover that a group's action on a tree with a finite set of branches is uniquely determined, given that the subgraphs inducing the branch structure on the tree's segments are all connected. This finding allows us to determine when actions on trees with finite sets of branches are equivalent and to identify the cases where actions on tree structures with finite sets of segments are not equivalent.

Nested Neumann algorithms are effective for solving large-scale linear systems, especially when dealing with systems that have positive semi-definite matrices. The performance of these algorithms can be improved by using a multi-level Nested Neumann approach, which relies on Nested Neumann algorithms to solve systems of systems. A key factor in this method is the Nested Neumann Inception Depth, which determines how many times Nested Neumann algorithms are used to solve systems of systems. A lower Nested Neumann Inception Depth results in faster convergence, but also requires more computational resources. A Nested Neumann algorithm is guaranteed to converge if the matrix is positive definite, but convergence rates can be slow for matrices with large condition numbers. A Nested Neumann Inception Depth of one is only feasible for systems that are easily solvable, which limits its practical use. A Nested Neumann Inception Depth of zero is only possible when systems of systems are already available, which is not always the case. A Nested Neumann Inception Depth of one is feasible when systems of systems are easily solvable, which is not always the case.
